# Interlude: The Orchard Patrol

**STATUS: DRAFT — Awaiting final approval**
**PLACEMENT: CONFIRMED — Between Chapter 5 (Planting & Growing) and Chapter 6 (Pests & Diseases)**
**Note: This is Randall's own writing. Do not edit without his instruction.**

---

One of the things visitors notice first when they come to my orchard isn't the fig trees.

It's the dogs.

The moment a vehicle starts down the driveway, the Great Pyrenees know about it long
before I do. Somewhere out among the rows of trees, a deep bark rolls across the property
like distant thunder, followed by another, then another. Within seconds, massive white
shapes emerge from the orchard itself — moving slowly, confidently, like they own every
inch of ground they walk on.

And truthfully, they probably believe they do.

Great Pyrenees are livestock guardian dogs by nature, bred for centuries to protect flocks
from wolves, bears, and predators in harsh mountain country. But here in Alabama, their
"flock" became my orchard, nursery, chickens, and family.

They patrol the property day and night.

Most people imagine an orchard as peaceful and quiet, and sometimes it is. Early mornings
can feel almost sacred — the sun just breaking through the trees, dew hanging on the
grass, figs swelling in the humid southern air. But orchards are living places, and living
places attract trouble. Raccoons. Coyotes. Stray dogs. Deer. Possums. Things that chew
irrigation lines, dig around roots, or decide ripe fruit belongs to them.

The Pyrenees take all of that personally.

What I've learned over time is that these dogs don't simply live at the orchard — they
become part of it. They know every path between the rows. They know when something is
different. They know when a vehicle belongs there and when it doesn't. At night, while
most people sleep, they make slow circles around the property line, stopping occasionally
to listen into the darkness before moving again.

There's something deeply comforting about walking the orchard late in the evening and
seeing a giant white dog silently appear between the fig trees like a ghost.

Sometimes they'll walk beside me for a while.

Sometimes they disappear back into the darkness without a sound.

Either way, you never really feel alone out there.

People often romanticize orchards — and I understand why. There's beauty in growing
things. There's peace in it. But orchards also require protection, discipline, and constant
attention. The dogs became part of that system naturally. Not because somebody trained
them to "guard fig trees," but because they instinctively understood this land belonged to
their family.

And in many ways, the orchard belongs to them too.

There are mornings when I'm checking cuttings or watering young trees and one of them
will stretch out right in the middle of the rows like a giant white bear, completely
unconcerned with productivity or schedules. Other times they'll suddenly explode into
barking because a hawk flew overhead or a coyote got too close during the night.

You learn to trust those instincts.

The older I get, the more I appreciate the atmosphere they create around the orchard.
It's hard to explain unless you've lived it yourself. There's something timeless about
dogs roaming beneath fruit trees while the sun rises over rows of plants you've spent
years building.

It feels old-world.

Almost biblical.

Sometimes I think about how orchards throughout history probably had their own guardians
too. Maybe not Great Pyrenees specifically, but animals and people watching over land that
fed families for generations. That same feeling still exists today, even in a modern
backyard nursery in Alabama.

And honestly, I can't imagine the orchard without them anymore.

They aren't just pets.

They're part of the story.
